blocks.html: In Simple Subject and Verb you learned to find the subject and the verb of a sentence, and in Is, Are, Was and Were you used is for one and are for more than one. Now we make every verb match its subject. This is called subject–verb agreement.

A singular subject (one) takes a singular verb. A plural subject (more than one) takes a plural verb. In the present tense, the singular verb for he, she, it or one thing usually ends in -s: “The dog barks.” The plural verb doesn’t: “The dogs bark.”

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: The dog barks at the mail truck.

blocks.cap: One dog, so the verb is barks.

head: Singular subject
Plural subject
blocks.cap: Be and have have their own forms. I and you use the plain form: I walk, you walk (but I am, you are).

blocks.html: A verb agrees with its subject in number: one dog barks, two dogs bark. Find the subject first, then choose the verb.
Agreement is a signal. The -s on barks tells the reader the subject is one thing, so the reader links the right words even in a long sentence. When a subject and verb disagree, the reader stumbles.

blocks.title: A plural without an -s
blocks.q: The children (play / plays) tag at recess.
steps: Find the subject: children.
Children means more than one child, so it is plural, even with no -s.
A plural subject takes the verb without -s: play.
blocks.a: The children play tag at recess.

blocks.title: Pronoun subjects
blocks.q: I (walk / walks) to school. She (walk / walks) with me.
steps: I and you take the plain form: I walk, you walk.
He, she and it take the -s form: she walks.
blocks.a: I walk to school. She walks with me.

blocks.html: Putting an -s on both words: “The dogs barks.” On a noun, -s usually means more than one. On a present-tense verb, -s goes with one. So the -s usually lands on one word or the other: “The dog barks” or “The dogs bark.” To check, say the sentence with it or they in place of the subject: “They bark.”

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.why: Birds is plural, so the verb is sing.
Feet is plural (one foot, two feet).
She takes has.
Mice is plural, so the verb is were.

blocks.cap: Sort each sentence: does the verb agree with its subject?

blocks.html: In Subject–Verb Agreement the subject sat right next to its verb. Often it doesn’t. A phrase can come between them, like the prepositional phrase of old crayons here:

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: The box of old crayons is on the shelf.

blocks.cap: Cross out the phrase: “The box … is on the shelf.”

blocks.html: The verb still agrees with the subject, box, not with crayons. A noun inside a prepositional phrase is the object of the preposition, and it is never the subject.
Cross out the phrase between the subject and the verb. Then read the subject and the verb together: “The box … is.”

Readers hold the subject in mind while they read the phrase. The verb then tells them which word was the subject all along. If the verb agrees with a nearby noun instead, it points the reader to the wrong word.

blocks.title: A plural noun in the phrase
blocks.q: The list of chores (is / are) on the fridge.
steps: Find the verb and ask who or what is/are on the fridge: the list.
Of chores is a prepositional phrase. Cross it out.
The list is.
blocks.a: The list of chores is on the fridge.

blocks.title: A singular noun in the phrase
blocks.q: The players on the team (has / have) new shirts.
steps: The subject is players, which is plural.
On the team is a phrase. Cross it out.
The players have.
blocks.a: The players on the team have new shirts.

blocks.title: Along with, as well as
blocks.q: The coach, along with her players, (was / were) on the bus.
steps: Phrases like along with, as well as and together with add extra information.
They don’t join subjects the way and does, so the subject is still coach.
The coach was.
blocks.a: The coach, along with her players, was on the bus.

blocks.html: Making the verb agree with the nearest noun: “The list of items are long.” Items is inside the phrase of items, so it can’t be the subject. Cross out the phrase and read what is left: “The list … is long.”

blocks.html: A compound subject has two or more parts joined by and, or or nor. The joining word decides the verb. Build on what you know from Subject–Verb Agreement.

items: And adds the parts into a group, so the verb is plural: “The cat and the dog are hungry.”
Or and nor pick one part, so the verb agrees with the part nearer to it: “Either the cats or the dog is hungry.” “Neither the dog nor the cats are hungry.”

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: Either the cats or the dog is hungry.

blocks.cap: With or, the verb looks at the subject closest to it: dog … is.

blocks.html: And makes a plural subject. With or or nor, the verb agrees with the subject closest to it.
And adds: two animals are hungry. Or chooses: only one of them is, and the verb matches the one beside it. Many writers put the plural part last, because “or the cats are” sounds smoother.

blocks.title: Joined by and
blocks.q: Pizza and salad (is / are) on the menu.
steps: Two things joined by and: pizza and salad.
Together they are plural.
blocks.a: Pizza and salad are on the menu.

blocks.title: Neither … nor
blocks.q: Neither my sister nor my brothers (like / likes) spinach.
steps: The parts are joined by nor, so look at the nearer part.
The nearer part is brothers, which is plural.
Brothers like.
blocks.a: Neither my sister nor my brothers like spinach.

blocks.title: Either … or, singular part last
blocks.q: Either the students or the teacher (has / have) the key.
steps: Nearer part: teacher, singular, so has.
If that sounds odd, switch the order: “Either the teacher or the students have the key.”
blocks.a: Either the students or the teacher has the key.

blocks.html: Treating or like and: “Either the cats or the dog are hungry.” With or or nor, only one part counts: the one closest to the verb. Point to it, then choose the verb.
One small exception: when two words joined by and name one thing, such as one dish, the verb is singular: “Macaroni and cheese is my favorite.”

blocks.html: An indefinite pronoun doesn’t name a particular person or thing: everyone, each, nobody, many. Some are always singular, some are always plural, and a few change. They often come with a phrase in between, as in Agreement Past a Phrase in Between.

head: Number
Pronouns
Example
rows: each, either, neither, one; everyone, everybody, everything; someone, somebody, something; anyone, anybody, anything; no one, nobody, nothing
“Some of the pie is gone.” “Some of the cookies are gone.”
blocks.cap: For some, all, most and any, look at the noun in the of phrase: a single amount or a group of things.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.why: Every one: one at a time.

blocks.cap: Sort the pronouns.

blocks.html: Words ending in -one, -body and -thing, and each, either and neither, are singular. Both, few, many and several are plural. Some, all, most and any follow the noun they refer to.
Everyone feels like a crowd, but the word looks at people one at a time: every one. That is why it takes is, just as one does.

blocks.title: Each with a phrase
blocks.q: Each of the students (has / have) a locker.
steps: The subject is each. Of the students is a phrase; cross it out.
Each is always singular.
blocks.a: Each of the students has a locker.

blocks.title: Most: it depends
blocks.q: Most of the water (is / are) cold. Most of the apples (is / are) ripe.
steps: Most follows the noun after of.
Water is one amount, so most is singular: is.
Apples are separate things, so most is plural: are.
blocks.a: Most of the water is cold. Most of the apples are ripe.

blocks.html: Collective nouns name a group: team, class, family, band, committee. In American English, a group acting as one unit usually takes a singular verb: “The team is winning.” British English often uses a plural verb: “The team are winning.” Each is standard in its own country. When the members act separately, American writers often say so: “The team members are arguing.” None varies too: “None of the cookies is left” and “None of the cookies are left” are both used by careful writers.
Using a plural verb after everyone or each because the idea feels like many people: “Everyone are here.” Count the word, not the crowd: every one is here.

blocks.html: Usually the subject comes before the verb. In Hard-to-Find Subjects you met sentences where it comes after: questions, and sentences that start with there or here. The agreement rules from Agreement with Compound Subjects still apply. You just have to look ahead for the subject.

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: There are two reasons for the delay.

blocks.cap: There is never the subject. The subject, reasons, comes after the verb.

blocks.html: When a sentence starts with there or here, or asks a question, find the subject after the verb and make the verb agree with it.
In these sentences the verb comes first, so the reader hears the number before seeing the subject. “There is …” promises one thing. If two things follow, the sentence breaks its promise.

blocks.title: There
blocks.q: There (is / are) three pencils in the cup.
steps: There is not the subject. What is in the cup? Three pencils.
Turn it around: “Three pencils are in the cup.”
blocks.a: There are three pencils in the cup.

blocks.title: A question
blocks.q: Where (is / are) my shoes?
steps: Make it a statement: “My shoes ___ where?”
The subject is shoes, plural.
blocks.a: Where are my shoes?

blocks.title: Here
blocks.q: Here (comes / come) the bus.
steps: Turn it around: “The bus comes here.”
Bus is singular.
blocks.a: Here comes the bus.

blocks.html: Writing “There’s two reasons.” Many people say there’s before a plural in conversation. Formal writing uses there are with a plural subject: “There are two reasons.” The same goes for where’s and here’s.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards, English Language Arts, Language standard L.3.1 (f: ensure subject–verb and pronoun–antecedent agreement), California Department of Education

blocks.html: Verbs agree with subjects. Pronouns agree too. A pronoun stands for a noun, and that noun is its antecedent (from Latin for “going before,” since it usually comes first). You already know the number rules from Indefinite Pronouns and Collective Nouns.

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: The girls packed their bags for the trip.

blocks.cap: Girls is plural, so the pronoun is their.

blocks.html: A pronoun agrees with its antecedent in number (one or more than one) and in person (first: I, we; second: you; third: he, she, it, they, one).
A pronoun matches the noun it stands for: one thing takes it or its, more than one takes they or their. Keep the same person all the way through.
A pronoun is a pointer. When its number or person doesn’t match, it points at nothing, or at the wrong thing, and the reader has to stop and search.

blocks.title: Number
blocks.q: The bikes lost (its / their) shine in the rain.
steps: The antecedent is bikes, plural.
A plural antecedent takes their.
blocks.a: The bikes lost their shine in the rain.

blocks.title: Person
blocks.q: When students study early, you remember more.
steps: Students is third person. You is second person: the sentence shifts.
Use a third-person pronoun for students: they.
blocks.a: When students study early, they remember more.

blocks.html: Shifting partway through: “If a person practices daily, you will improve.” Pick one and keep it: “If you practice daily, you will improve,” or “People who practice daily improve.” (For a single person whose gender you don’t know, see Singular They and Generic Pronouns.)

blocks.html: In Pronoun–Antecedent Agreement the antecedent told you which pronoun to use. Sometimes it doesn’t: “Each student should bring ___ notebook.” The student could be anyone. Writers have four good choices here:

items: Singular they: “Each student should bring their notebook.”
He or she: “Each student should bring his or her notebook.”
A plural rewrite: “Students should bring their notebooks.”
A rewrite with no pronoun: “Each student should bring a notebook.”

blocks.name: wr-revise

opts.before: Each student should bring his or her notebook to class.
opts.after: All students should bring their notebooks to class.
opts.title: A plural rewrite

blocks.cap: Making the antecedent plural removes the question.

blocks.html: Singular they is old. The Oxford English Dictionary’s earliest example of they for an unknown person dates from about 1375. Some grammarians of the 1700s objected to it and recommended he, and schools taught that for a long time. Today the guides differ: APA (7th edition), MLA (9th edition) and Chicago (18th edition) accept singular they; the AP Stylebook allows it in limited cases, when other wording would be awkward; and some teachers and editors still prefer a rewrite.
For a person whose gender is unknown or not the point, you may use singular they, he or she, or a rewrite. Each is standard; find out which one your teacher or style guide prefers.
Readers notice pronouns. He alone for everyone leaves people out, and he or she again and again gets heavy. Choosing well keeps the reader’s attention on your ideas.

blocks.title: Three ways to write it
blocks.q: If a visitor arrives early, ___ can wait in the lobby.
steps: Singular they: “… they can wait in the lobby.”
He or she: “… he or she can wait in the lobby.”
Plural rewrite: “Visitors who arrive early can wait in the lobby.”
blocks.a: All three are standard. Choose by your guide, and by what reads best.

blocks.title: The verb with singular they
blocks.q: Someone left a note, and (they is / they are) waiting for an answer.
steps: Singular they keeps its plural verb forms, the way you does when you talk to one person (“you are”).
blocks.a: … and they are waiting for an answer.

blocks.html: Learning one choice as the only correct one. Singular they, he or she, and a rewrite are all standard; style guides differ on which they prefer. What doesn’t change: singular they takes are, were and have, never is, was or has.

blocks.html: A pronoun works only when the reader knows which noun it points to, its antecedent from Pronoun–Antecedent Agreement. Read this:

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: When Ana called Mia, she was upset.

blocks.cap: Who was upset, Ana or Mia? Both fit, so the pronoun is unclear.

blocks.html: Two kinds of pronoun trouble cause most unclear sentences: two possible antecedents, as above, and no antecedent at all, as in “They say it will rain,” where nobody says who they are.

items: Repeat the noun: “When Ana called Mia, Mia was upset.”
Rearrange: “Ana was upset when she called Mia.”
Name what this or it means: “This delay made us late.”
Say who they are: “The forecast says it will rain.”

blocks.html: Each pronoun should point to one clear noun. If two nouns could fit, or none does, use the noun itself.
You know what you meant; the reader has only the page. A vague pronoun makes the reader guess, and readers often guess wrong.

blocks.title: A loose this
blocks.q: The bus was late, and it rained all morning. This made us grumpy.
steps: What does this point to: the bus, the rain, or both?
Name it.
blocks.a: The late bus and the rain made us grumpy.

blocks.title: Two people
blocks.q: Dad told Grandpa that his car was ready.
steps: Whose car: Dad’s or Grandpa’s?
Say it outright.
blocks.a: Dad told Grandpa, “Your car is ready.” (or: “My car is ready.”)

blocks.name: wr-revise

segments.why: Name the person, so the reader knows who was upset.

blocks.cap: One word fixes it.

blocks.html: Using this, it or they with nothing definite to point to: “They say it will rain.” “This shows that …” Ask: what, exactly, does the pronoun stand for? If you have to think, write the noun.

blocks.html: In Personal and Possessive Pronouns you met I, me, she, her and the rest. In Direct Objects you found the word that receives the action. Now put the two together: a pronoun changes its form to show its job. That form is called its case.

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: She called him after lunch.

blocks.cap: She does the calling (subject); him receives it (object).

head: Case
Pronouns
Job
Example
rows: I, he, she, we, they, who
me, him, her, us, them, whom
object of a verb or a preposition
my, mine, his, her, hers, our, ours, their, theirs, whose
blocks.cap: You and it are the same as subjects and objects.

blocks.html: Use subject pronouns (I, he, she, we, they) as subjects. Use object pronouns (me, him, her, us, them) after verbs and prepositions.
English shows a pronoun’s job by its form. “Him called she” has the right words in the wrong forms, and it sounds broken because the forms are what tell the reader who did what.

blocks.title: A subject
blocks.q: (Them / They) won the game.
steps: Who won? The pronoun is the subject.
Subjects take the subject form: they.
blocks.a: They won the game.

blocks.title: After a preposition
blocks.q: Coach gave the trophy to (we / us).
steps: To is a preposition, and the pronoun is its object.
Objects take the object form: us.
blocks.a: Coach gave the trophy to us.

blocks.html: Using an object pronoun as a subject when there are two people: “Me and Sam went to the park.” Take Sam out: “Me went” sounds wrong, “I went” sounds right. So: “Sam and I went to the park.” (Putting the other person first is a courtesy.) The next topic, Pronouns in Pairs, practices this test.

After is and was, traditional formal grammar uses the subject form (“It is I.” “This is she.”), while “It’s me” is normal in conversation and accepted by many usage guides. Both are heard; very formal writing keeps the subject form.

blocks.html: In Subject and Object Pronouns each pronoun stood alone. When a pronoun shares its job with another person, ears get confused. Here is a test that always works: take out the other person and read the pronoun alone.

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: Grandma took Sam and me to the zoo.

blocks.cap: Cross out “Sam and”: Grandma took me. So: Grandma took Sam and me.

head: The pair
Take out the other person
So
rows: The gift is for Sam and (I / me).

blocks.html: Cover the other person (or the noun after we or us) and read the pronoun alone. The form that sounds right alone is right in the pair.
Each pronoun in a pair has the same job it would have alone. In “Sam and I went,” both are subjects. In “for Sam and me,” both are objects of the preposition for.

blocks.title: An object pair
blocks.q: The teacher chose Lily and (I / me).
steps: Take out Lily: “The teacher chose ___.”
“Chose me” sounds right, because the pronoun receives the choosing.
blocks.a: The teacher chose Lily and me.

blocks.title: Between
blocks.q: Between you and (I / me), the quiz was hard.
steps: Between is a preposition. Both you and the pronoun are its objects.
Objects take the object form: me.
blocks.a: Between you and me, the quiz was hard.

blocks.title: He and I
blocks.q: (Him and me / He and I) built the model.
steps: Test each one alone: “He built it.” “I built it.”
Both are subjects.
blocks.a: He and I built the model.

blocks.html: Overcorrecting. People who were told not to say “Me and Sam went” sometimes use I everywhere because it sounds polite: “between you and I,” “a gift for Sam and I.” I is only for subjects. Take the other person out and listen: “a gift for I” is clearly wrong.

blocks.html: Who and whom have case, just like the pairs in Pronouns in Pairs: who is a subject, like he; whom is an object, like him. They often start the adjective clauses you studied in Grammar, and they start many questions.

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: The friend whom I invited came.

blocks.cap: Inside its own clause, whom is the object of invited: I invited him.

blocks.html: The he/him test. Turn the question or the clause into a short statement, and put in he or him. If him fits, use whom; both end in m.
Who does what a subject does (he); whom receives an action or follows a preposition (him). Choose by the word’s job inside its own clause, not by the words around it.
In a long sentence, who and whom tell the reader how the clause is built: who did the action and who received it.

blocks.title: A clause in the middle
blocks.q: Our coach, (who / whom) everyone admires, is retiring.
steps: Take the clause alone: “everyone admires ___.”
Everyone admires him: an object.
blocks.a: Our coach, whom everyone admires, is retiring.

blocks.title: After a preposition, but a subject
blocks.q: Give the prize to (whoever / whomever) finishes first.
steps: To comes first, which tempts you toward whomever.
But inside its clause the word is the subject of finishes: he finishes first.
The whole clause is the object of to.
blocks.a: Give the prize to whoever finishes first.

blocks.title: Words in between
blocks.q: (Who / Whom) do you think will win?
steps: Set aside do you think: “___ will win?”
He will win: a subject.
blocks.a: Who do you think will win?

blocks.html: Choosing by the nearby words instead of the word’s job in its own clause, as in “to whomever finishes.” Also know the range: many people use who for both in conversation (“Who did you call?”), and that is normal speech. Formal writing keeps whom for objects.

blocks.html: The -self words are myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves and themselves. You met them in Other Kinds of Pronouns. They have two proper jobs, and both need a word earlier in the sentence to point back to. (Compare Subject and Object Pronouns.)

items: Reflexive: the subject acts on itself. “I hurt myself.” “The cat washed itself.”
Intensive: for emphasis. “I painted the fence myself.” “The author herself signed my copy.”

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: Maya taught herself to juggle.

blocks.cap: Herself points back to the subject, Maya.

blocks.html: Use a -self word only when it refers back to the subject or adds emphasis. Otherwise use I or me (he or him, and so on).

A -self word tells the reader that the same person is doing and receiving: “I hurt myself.” Used anywhere else, it sends a false signal, as if someone earlier in the sentence were being pointed back to.

blocks.title: No subject to point back to
blocks.q: Please send the photos to Sam or (me / myself).
steps: The subject is an understood you, not I.
Nothing for myself to point back to, so use the object form after to.
blocks.a: Please send the photos to Sam or me.

blocks.title: A subject pair
blocks.q: Sam and (I / myself) planned the party.
steps: Take out Sam: “I planned the party.”
blocks.a: Sam and I planned the party.

blocks.title: Standard forms
blocks.q: The twins built the fort by (theirselves / themselves).
steps: Many people say hisself and theirselves in conversation.
Standard written English uses himself and themselves.
blocks.a: The twins built the fort by themselves.

blocks.html: Using myself to sound polite or formal: “Please send it to Sam or myself.” “Jo and myself will lead.” Test it: take out the other person. “Send it to myself” and “Myself will lead” don’t work, so use me and I.

blocks.html: In Yesterday, Today, Tomorrow you told when things happen. In Helping Verbs and Verb Phrases you met will, have and be as helpers. A verb’s tense shows time. The three simple tenses are the base of all the others.

blocks.name: wr-tense
blocks.cap: Tap past, present and future to move along the timeline.

head: Tense
Form
Use
Time words
rows: habits, facts and what is true now

blocks.html: Spelling the past with -ed: hope → hoped (just add -d after e); stop → stopped (one vowel, one consonant: double it); carry → carried (consonant + y: change y to i); play → played (vowel + y: just add -ed).
Use the simple past for a finished action, the simple present for habits and facts, and will + the verb for the future.
Tense puts events on a timeline. A reader who sees walked knows it is over; walks says it happens regularly; will walk says it hasn’t happened yet.

blocks.title: A time word
blocks.q: Last summer we (visit) the lake.
steps: Last summer is finished time.
Use the simple past: visit + -ed.
blocks.a: Last summer we visited the lake.

blocks.title: A fact
blocks.q: At sea level, water (boil) at 212°F.
steps: This is always true, not one event.
Facts and habits use the simple present; water is singular, so add -s.
blocks.a: At sea level, water boils at 212°F.

blocks.title: Spelling
blocks.q: Write the simple past of stop and carry.
steps: Stop ends in one vowel and one consonant: double the p.
Carry ends in consonant + y: change y to i and add -ed.
blocks.a: stopped, carried

blocks.html: Thinking English has only three tenses. The simple tenses are the base; the progressive (I am walking) and the perfect (I have walked) add shades of time, for twelve forms in all. (Some grammar books count only past and present as true tenses and call will a helping verb; school grammars usually count all twelve.)

blocks.html: In The Simple Tenses you added -ed to make the past. Verbs that do that are regular. Many of the most common verbs are irregular: they make their past forms in their own ways.
Every verb has three main forms, its principal parts: the base (go), the past (went), and the past participle (gone), which follows has, have or had.

head: Base
Past
Past participle
blocks.cap: A dictionary lists the principal parts of every irregular verb.

blocks.name: wr-sort
blocks.cap: Which forms stand alone, and which need a helper?

blocks.html: The past stands alone (I saw it). The past participle needs a helper (I have seen it). For irregular verbs, learn all three parts.
These are the verbs we use most, so readers notice them. The right form also tells the time: I saw is a finished event, I have seen links the past to now.

blocks.title: Past, no helper
blocks.q: Yesterday I (see) a hawk.
steps: No helper, finished time: use the past.
The past of see is saw.
blocks.a: Yesterday I saw a hawk.

blocks.title: With a helper
blocks.q: She has (go) home.
steps: Has is a helper, so use the past participle.
The past participle of go is gone.
blocks.a: She has gone home.

blocks.title: No -ed
blocks.q: He (bring) snacks for everyone.
steps: Bring is irregular: bring, brought, brought.
blocks.a: He brought snacks for everyone.

blocks.html: Using the past participle as the past (“I seen it,” “she done it”) or adding -ed to an irregular verb (“bringed”). People say these in everyday speech in many places. Standard written English uses saw and did alone, or have seen and has done with a helper.

blocks.html: The simple tenses show that something happens. The progressive tenses show that it is in progress: going on at some moment. They use a form of be plus the -ing form of the verb.

blocks.name: wr-tense
blocks.cap: Compare simple and progressive at each time.

head: Tense
Form
Example
rows: I was reading when the phone rang.
We will be reading at noon tomorrow.

blocks.html: Spelling -ing: make → making (drop a silent e); run → running (double after one vowel and one consonant); lie → lying (ie becomes y).
A form of be + an -ing verb shows an action in progress: I am reading, I was reading, I will be reading.
The progressive sets a scene: an action going on in the background while something else happens. “I was reading when the phone rang” shows a long action interrupted by a short one.

blocks.title: Right now
blocks.q: Right now the twins (play) chess.
steps: Right now: in progress in the present.
Twins is plural, so use are + playing.
blocks.a: Right now the twins are playing chess.

blocks.title: Background and interruption
blocks.q: We (walk) home when it (start) to rain.
steps: The long action, walking, was in progress: past progressive, were walking.
The rain started at one moment: simple past, started.
blocks.a: We were walking home when it started to rain.

blocks.html: Using the progressive for states that aren’t actions: “I am knowing the answer.” Verbs like know, believe, belong, own, need and seem usually take the simple form: “I know the answer.” A few verbs have both an action meaning and a state meaning: “I am having lunch” (eating), but “I have a bike” (owning).

sources.name: Common Core State Standards, English Language Arts, Language standard L.4.1 (b: form and use the progressive verb tenses), California Department of Education
Purdue OWL (Purdue University Online Writing Lab), “Active Verb Tenses”
Grokipedia, “Grammatical aspect”

blocks.html: The perfect tenses use a form of have plus a past participle, the third principal part from Irregular Verbs. Like the progressive tenses, they add a shade of time: an action finished before some point.

blocks.name: wr-tense
blocks.cap: The perfect tenses look back from a point in time.

head: Tense
Form
Use
Example
rows: from the past up to now, with no finished time named
I have read three books this month.
When we arrived, the movie had started.
By June, she will have finished the quilt.

blocks.html: Have + past participle looks back: has eaten (up to now), had eaten (before another past time), will have eaten (before a future time).
The perfect tenses keep events in order. “When we arrived, the movie started” means it began as we walked in. “When we arrived, the movie had started” means we missed the beginning.

blocks.title: Finished time or not?
blocks.q: I (see) that movie yesterday. I (see) it twice.
steps: Yesterday names a finished time: simple past, saw.
“Twice,” with no time named, counts up to now: present perfect, have seen.
blocks.a: I saw that movie yesterday. I have seen it twice.

blocks.title: Two past events
blocks.q: By the time we reached the station, the train (leave).
steps: Two past events: we reached the station; the train left.
The train left first, so it takes the past perfect.
blocks.a: … the train had left.

blocks.title: Before a future time
blocks.q: By next Friday, I (finish) my project.
steps: The finishing will be done before a future point, next Friday.
Use will have + finished.
blocks.a: By next Friday, I will have finished my project.

blocks.html: Putting a finished time with the present perfect (“I have seen it yesterday”): use the simple past, “I saw it yesterday.” And using the simple past where the past perfect shows which of two past events came first.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards, English Language Arts, Language standard L.5.1 (b: form and use the perfect verb tenses), California Department of Education
Purdue OWL (Purdue University Online Writing Lab), “Active Verb Tenses”
Grokipedia, “Perfect (grammar)”

blocks.html: You now know the simple, progressive and perfect tenses. When you write a paragraph, choose a main tense, usually the past for a story, and stay in it. Change tense only when the time really changes.

blocks.name: wr-revise

segments.why: The story is in the past, so keep this verb in the past.

segments: a puppy on the step. It

segments.why: Same moment as opened and saw: past.

blocks.cap: Two verbs slipped into the present. Fixed.

blocks.html: Stay in one tense unless the time really changes.
A change of tense is a signal that time has moved. If the time didn’t move, the signal misleads: the reader wonders whether the puppy wagged its tail now or back then.

blocks.title: An accidental shift
blocks.q: We hiked to the top, and then we eat lunch.
steps: Hiked sets the story in the past.
Eat slips into the present, though the lunch happened then too.
blocks.a: We hiked to the top, and then we ate lunch.

blocks.title: A real change of time
blocks.q: Last year I lived in Ohio, but now I live in Texas.
steps: Last year is past; now is present.
The time really changes, so the tense changes too.
blocks.a: Correct as written.

blocks.html: One convention to know: when you write about a book or a story, use the present tense, called the literary present: “In the fable, the fox flatters the crow.” The story is always there on the page, happening each time it is read.

Sliding from past to present in the middle of a story, often when it gets exciting: “The lights went out, and suddenly someone grabs my arm.” Read your draft and underline each verb. If the time didn’t change, the tense shouldn’t either.

blocks.html: Three pairs of irregular verbs trip up careful writers. In each pair, one verb takes a direct object (you put or lift something) and the other doesn’t.

head: Verb
Meaning
Past
Past participle
-ing
blocks.cap: Lie meaning “tell an untruth” is a different verb: lie, lied, lied.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.text: Lay the map on the table.
cards.why: You lay something: the map.

cards.text: The cat lies in the sun.
Set your bag by the door.

blocks.cap: Is something being put or lifted?

blocks.html: Ask: is something being put or lifted? If yes, use lay, set or raise. If not, use lie, sit or rise.
The two verbs in each pair mean different things. “The hen lays” (an egg) and “The hen lies down” describe different events, so choosing the right one keeps your meaning exact.

blocks.title: No object, present
blocks.q: Every afternoon the dog (lies / lays) on the porch.
steps: Is the dog putting something down? No. It is resting.
No object: lie. With dog, lies.
blocks.a: Every afternoon the dog lies on the porch.

blocks.title: No object, past
blocks.q: Yesterday I (lay / laid) down for a nap.
steps: Nothing is being put down: the verb is lie.
The past of lie is lay.
blocks.a: Yesterday I lay down for a nap.

blocks.title: An object, past
blocks.q: She (lay / laid) the baby in the crib.
steps: She put something down: the baby. That is an object.
The verb is lay; its past is laid.
blocks.a: She laid the baby in the crib.

blocks.html: Mixing the forms because the past of lie is lay. Many people use lay for both verbs in conversation (“I’m going to lay down”). Formal writing keeps them apart: “I’m going to lie down.” Ask: is something being put somewhere?

sources.name: Purdue OWL (Purdue University Online Writing Lab), “Commonly Confused Verbs”
Common Core State Standards, English Language Arts, Language standard L.3.1 (d: form and use regular and irregular verbs), California Department of Education

blocks.html: In the active voice, the subject does the action: “Sam threw the ball.” In the passive voice, the subject receives the action: “The ball was thrown by Sam.” The direct object of the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive one. The passive uses a form of be plus a past participle (from Perfect Tenses).

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: The ball was thrown by Sam.

blocks.cap: A passive sentence: the ball receives the action, and Sam, the doer, comes after by.

head: Active
Passive
rows: The ball was thrown by Sam.
The roof was damaged by the storm.
blocks.cap: In a passive sentence the doer may be left out altogether.

blocks.html: Active: the subject acts. Passive: the subject receives the action, and the verb is a form of be + a past participle.

Strunk’s rule 10 (1918) says, “The active voice is usually more direct and vigorous than the passive.” But the passive is the right choice when the doer is unknown or doesn’t matter: “My bike was stolen.” “The winners will be announced on Friday.”

blocks.title: Is it passive?
blocks.q: The window was broken by a baseball.
steps: Was + broken: a form of be + a past participle.
The window doesn’t act; it receives the action.
blocks.a: Passive.

blocks.title: A was that isn’t passive
blocks.q: The sky was blue.
steps: Was is a linking verb here, and blue is an adjective, not a past participle.
Nothing is being done to the sky.
blocks.a: Not passive.

blocks.title: Make it active
blocks.q: The cake was baked by Grandma.
steps: Find the doer, after by: Grandma.
Make the doer the subject, and the receiver the object.
blocks.a: Grandma baked the cake.

blocks.html: Thinking any sentence with was or is is passive, or that the passive is a grammar error. “She was running” is active (the progressive). The passive is a correct form of the verb; the question is only whether it is the best choice for the sentence.

blocks.html: After tense and voice, verbs have one more feature: mood. Mood shows how the writer presents the action: as a fact, as a command, or as something wished for or not real.

head: Mood
What it does
Example
rows: wishes, conditions that aren’t true, and demands or requests after that
“If I were taller …” “I wish it were Friday.” “The coach asks that every player arrive on time.”
blocks.cap: The Common Core standard also names interrogative and conditional moods; many grammar books count questions as indicative and treat would sentences as conditional.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.text: If I were you, I would rest.
cards.why: Were for an unreal condition: I am not you.
Questions are usually counted as indicative.

blocks.cap: Sort the sentences by mood.

blocks.html: For a wish or a condition that isn’t true, formal writing uses were with every subject: if I were, if she were. After verbs like ask, insist and require + that, it uses the base form: that she be, that he arrive.
Were signals “not true.” “If I were a bird” tells the reader you are not one, while “If I was late yesterday, I’m sorry” treats being late as a real possibility.

blocks.title: An unreal condition
blocks.q: If I (was / were) a bird, I would fly south.
steps: I am not a bird: the condition is unreal.
Use the subjunctive were.
blocks.a: If I were a bird, I would fly south.

blocks.title: A real possibility
blocks.q: If she (was / were) at the game yesterday, she saw the goal.
steps: We don’t know whether she was there; it may well be true.
A real possibility takes the indicative was.
blocks.a: If she was at the game yesterday, she saw the goal.

blocks.title: A requirement
blocks.q: The rules require that every rider (wear / wears) a helmet.
steps: Require that calls for the subjunctive.
The subjunctive is the base form, with no -s.
blocks.a: … that every rider wear a helmet. (British English often says “should wear.”)

blocks.html: Writing “If I was taller” in formal writing. Was there is common in conversation; the subjunctive were is standard in formal writing for a condition that isn’t true.

Purdue OWL (Purdue University Online Writing Lab), “Verbs: Voice and Mood”
Grokipedia, “English subjunctive”

blocks.html: Adjectives and adverbs can compare. The comparative compares two things: taller, more careful. The superlative compares three or more: tallest, most careful.

head: Kind of word
Comparative
Superlative
rows: two syllables ending in y: happy
blocks.cap: A few two-syllable words take either form (quieter or more quiet). When in doubt, check a dictionary.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.text: the tallest player on the team
the best day of the year
the most careful driver of all

blocks.cap: Two things, or a group?

blocks.html: Use -er or more to compare two, and -est or most for three or more. Use one or the other, never both, and learn the irregular forms: good, better, best.
The ending tells the reader how big the group is. “The taller twin” is one of two; “the tallest girl” stands out in a crowd.

blocks.title: Two things
blocks.q: Of the two puppies, the brown one is (smaller / smallest).
steps: Two puppies: use the comparative.
blocks.a: Of the two puppies, the brown one is smaller.

blocks.title: A long word, a group
blocks.q: This is the (more / most) exciting book in the series.
steps: A series has many books: use the superlative.
Exciting is a long word, so use most.
blocks.a: This is the most exciting book in the series.

blocks.title: Irregular
blocks.q: My second try was (more better / better) than my first.
steps: Better is already the comparative of good.
Adding more doubles the comparison.
blocks.a: My second try was better than my first.

blocks.html: Doubling up (“more taller,” “most fastest”) or using the superlative for two (“the tallest of the twins”). Count the group: two takes -er or more; three or more takes -est or most. Then use just one marker.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards, English Language Arts, Language standard L.3.1 (g: form and use comparative and superlative adjectives and adverbs), California Department of Education
University of Victoria English Language Centre Study Zone, “Comparatives and Superlatives”

blocks.html: Adjectives describe nouns. Adverbs describe verbs, adjectives and other adverbs. Most of the time that is easy. Two places cause trouble: good and well, and the linking verbs. Build on Comparing with Adjectives and Adverbs.

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: The soup smells good. Dad cooks well.

blocks.cap: Good describes the soup (a noun); well describes how Dad cooks (a verb).

items: Good is an adjective: a good game. Well is usually an adverb: she played well.
After a linking verb (be, seem, feel, look, smell, taste, sound, become), the word describes the subject, so it is an adjective: “I feel bad.” “The soup smells good.”
After an action verb, use an adverb: “She sings well.” “Drive carefully.”
A few words work both ways with no -ly: fast, hard, late (“She runs fast”).

blocks.html: Ask what the word describes. A thing or a person (or the subject after a linking verb): adjective. An action: adverb.
The two forms mean different things. “The dog smells bad” means it needs a bath. “The dog smells badly” would mean its nose doesn’t work well.

blocks.title: How did you do?
blocks.q: You did (good / well) on the quiz.
steps: The word describes how you did: an action.
Actions take the adverb: well.
blocks.a: You did well on the quiz.

blocks.title: A linking verb
blocks.q: I feel (bad / badly) about the mix-up.
steps: Feel links the subject to a description of it.
The word describes I, so use the adjective bad.
blocks.a: I feel bad about the mix-up.

blocks.title: Same verb, two jobs
blocks.q: The dog sniffed (careful / carefully). The milk smelled (sour / sourly).
steps: Sniffed is an action: carefully tells how.
Smelled here links the milk to a description: sour describes the milk.
blocks.a: The dog sniffed carefully. The milk smelled sour.

blocks.html: Writing “did good” for “did well,” or overcorrecting to “I feel badly.” Many people say “I feel badly” in conversation to mean they regret something; formal writing uses “I feel bad.” Well is also an adjective about health: “I feel well” (not sick). “I feel good” and “I feel well” are both standard.

Purdue OWL (Purdue University Online Writing Lab), “Avoiding Common Errors (adjective or adverb)”
Grokipedia, “Flat adverb”

blocks.html: Negative words say no: no, not (and -n’t), never, nobody, nothing, none, nowhere, neither. A few hide their meaning: hardly, scarcely and barely are negatives too. Like good and well, these words follow a rule of standard writing: one negative per idea.

blocks.name: wr-revise

segments.why: One negative word is enough: don’t.

blocks.cap: Two fixes, one negative each.

head: Two negatives
Standard written English
rows: I didn’t see anybody. / I saw nobody.
She will never quit. / She won’t ever quit.
They don’t have any. / They have none.

blocks.html: Standard written English uses one negative word per idea: “I don’t have any,” or “I have none.”
Readers of formal writing expect one negative, and some read two as canceling out: “I didn’t see nobody” could seem to mean you saw somebody. One negative keeps the meaning certain.

This is a rule of standard writing, not of English everywhere. Older English stacked negatives for force: Chaucer wrote of his knight, “He nevere yet no vileynye ne sayde” (General Prologue, The Canterbury Tales), meaning he never said anything rude. Grammar books of the 1700s argued that two negatives cancel each other, and the one-negative rule became the standard for writing. Many dialects of English still use double negatives in speech, following their own regular pattern.

blocks.title: Choose the standard form
blocks.q: There isn’t (nothing / anything) in the box.
steps: Isn’t is already negative.
So the second word should be the positive anything.
blocks.a: There isn’t anything in the box.

blocks.title: A hidden negative
blocks.q: I (can / can’t) hardly hear you.
steps: Hardly means “almost not.” It is a negative.
Use the positive can.
blocks.a: I can hardly hear you.

blocks.html: Missing the hidden negatives hardly, scarcely and barely: “can’t hardly,” “couldn’t scarcely.” When one of these is in the sentence, leave out not.

blocks.html: A modifier describes another word. Prepositional phrases and participial phrases are modifiers too, and they attach to the nearest word they could describe. Put a modifier in the wrong place and it describes the wrong thing.

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: She gave cake to kids on paper plates.

blocks.cap: The phrase sits next to kids, so it seems to describe them.

blocks.name: wr-picture

frames.caption: What it says: kids on plates.
What we meant: cake on plates.

blocks.cap: Move the phrase next to cake: “She gave cake on paper plates to the kids.”

blocks.html: Limiting words such as only, just, almost and even go right before the word they limit, and moving them changes the meaning: “Only Sam ate the pie” (nobody else did). “Sam ate only the pie” (he ate nothing else).
Put a modifier next to the word it describes. Put only, just and almost right before the word they limit.
Readers attach a modifier to the closest word it could describe. They can’t ask you what you meant, so the sentence has to say it.

blocks.title: Move the phrase
blocks.q: Dad bought a hat for my mom with a feather.
steps: The feather belongs to the hat, not to Mom.
Move with a feather next to hat.
blocks.a: Dad bought a hat with a feather for my mom.

blocks.title: Only
blocks.q: Which sentence says that Lena, and nobody else, passed? “Lena only passed the test.” / “Only Lena passed the test.”
steps: Only limits the word right after it.
To limit Lena, put only before Lena.
blocks.a: “Only Lena passed the test.”

blocks.html: Leaving a phrase where it lands on the wrong noun: “She gave cake to kids on paper plates.” Read the sentence once looking only at the phrase: what does it sit next to? Move it beside the word it really describes. In conversation, people often put only before the verb (“I only have five dollars”); in careful writing, put it before the word it limits: “I have only five dollars.”

sources.name: Common Core State Standards, English Language Arts, Language standard L.7.1 (c: place phrases and clauses within a sentence, recognizing and correcting misplaced and dangling modifiers), California Department of Education
Northern Illinois University, Effective Writing Practices Tutorial, “Misplaced Modifiers”

blocks.html: A misplaced modifier sits next to the wrong word. A dangling modifier has no right word at all. An opening phrase describes the subject that comes right after its comma. If that subject can’t do what the phrase says, the modifier dangles.

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: Walking home, a fox appeared.

blocks.cap: By the grammar, the fox was walking home.

blocks.name: wr-picture

frames.caption: What it says: a fox walking home.
What we meant: I was walking home and saw a fox.

blocks.cap: Name the walker.

blocks.html: Strunk’s rule 7 (1918) puts it this way: “A participial phrase at the beginning of a sentence must refer to the grammatical subject.” One of his examples: “Young and inexperienced, the task seemed easy to me” becomes “Young and inexperienced, I thought the task easy.”

items: Make the doer the subject: “Walking home, I saw a fox.”
Give the phrase its own subject: “As I was walking home, a fox appeared.”

blocks.html: An opening phrase must describe the subject that comes right after it. If it doesn’t, name the doer as the subject, or turn the phrase into a clause.
Readers follow the grammar, not your intentions. A dangling modifier makes the sentence say something odd, and the reader laughs or stops to fix it.

blocks.title: After finishing
blocks.q: After finishing the test, the bell rang.
steps: Who finished the test? Not the bell.
Give the phrase a subject, or make the doer the subject.
blocks.a: After we finished the test, the bell rang. (or: After finishing the test, we heard the bell.)

blocks.title: An infinitive phrase
blocks.q: To win the race, practice is needed.
steps: Who wants to win? Practice can’t.
Name the person who will practice.
blocks.a: To win the race, you need practice.

blocks.html: Assuming the reader knows who was doing the action. The writer knows it was “I” walking home; the grammar says the fox was. After writing an opening phrase, look at the very next noun or pronoun and ask: can it do this?

blocks.html: In Commas in a List you put commas between things in a list. Now we can say it more exactly. A series is three or more words, phrases or clauses in a row, joined at the end by and or or. Commas mark the border between one item and the next, the way your voice pauses when you read a list aloud.

blocks.name: wr-punct

opts.text: We packed sandwiches apples and lemonade for the picnic.
answer: We packed sandwiches, apples, and lemonade for the picnic.
We packed sandwiches, apples and lemonade for the picnic.
opts.why: Both versions count: with or without the comma before and.

blocks.cap: Add the commas to the series. Either style counts.

blocks.html: Put a comma after each item in a series except the last. The comma just before and or or is called the serial (or Oxford) comma, and it is a style choice.

head: Style guide
Comma before the last and?
rows: Usually no, unless leaving it out would confuse
blocks.cap: Both styles are standard. Pick one and use it the same way all through a piece.

blocks.html: Without commas, the items blur together: “We bought pears plums peaches and grapes” makes the reader sort out the words. Back in 1918, William Strunk’s second rule said it plainly: “In a series of three or more terms with a single conjunction, use a comma after each term except the last.”

blocks.title: A series of actions
blocks.q: Add commas: “Mia can sing dance and play the drums.”
steps: Find the items: sing / dance / play the drums. There are three, so it is a series.
Put a comma after each item except the last.
With the serial comma: “Mia can sing, dance, and play the drums.”
Without it (AP style): “Mia can sing, dance and play the drums.”
blocks.a: Mia can sing, dance, and play the drums. (Leaving out the comma before and is also standard.)

blocks.title: When the last comma prevents confusion
blocks.q: “For lunch we had soup, salad and macaroni and cheese.”
steps: The items are soup / salad / macaroni and cheese. The last item has its own and.
Without the serial comma, “salad and macaroni and cheese” runs together.
Here even AP style adds the comma.
blocks.a: For lunch we had soup, salad, and macaroni and cheese.

blocks.html: Being told the serial comma is simply right or simply wrong. It is a choice between two standard styles; school papers in MLA style use it. The real errors are a comma after the last item (“apples, and lemonade, for the picnic”) and a comma between only two items (“sandwiches, and apples”). Two items need no comma at all.

Grokipedia, “Serial comma”
William Strunk Jr., The Elements of Style (1918; public domain, Project Gutenberg #37134), rule 2
Common Core State Standards for English Language Arts, Language standard L.5.2a: use punctuation to separate items in a series (California Department of Education edition, PDF)

blocks.html: Some commas follow custom more than meaning. You will use them in every letter and email: in dates, between a city and its state, after yes and no, before a short tag question, and around the name of someone you are speaking to (direct address). They build on commas in a series.

items: Dates: “On May 4, 2025, the library opened.” A month and year alone take no comma: “in May 2025.”
Places: “We drove from Akron, Ohio, to Erie.”
Yes and no: “Yes, I can come.” “No, thank you.”
Tag questions: “It’s cold today, isn’t it?”
Direct address: “Thanks, Sam.” “Sam, can you help?” “I think, Sam, that you’re right.”

blocks.name: wr-punct

opts.text: On July 4 1776 the Continental Congress approved the Declaration of Independence.
answer: On July 4, 1776, the Continental Congress approved the Declaration of Independence.

blocks.cap: A date in the middle of a sentence: add the two commas.

blocks.html: Use a comma between the day and the year and between a city and its state. When the date or place sits in the middle of a sentence, put a comma after the year or state too. Set off yes, no, tag questions and the name of the person you are speaking to.

These commas keep numbers and names from running together (“July 4 1776”) and show who is being spoken to. The old joke says it best: “Let’s eat, Grandma!” invites Grandma to dinner. “Let’s eat Grandma!” is a very different plan.

blocks.title: A place in the middle of a sentence
blocks.q: Add commas: “We moved to Boise Idaho in June.”
steps: Boise is the city and Idaho is the state: comma between them.
The sentence keeps going after Idaho, so the state gets a comma after it too.
blocks.a: We moved to Boise, Idaho, in June.

blocks.title: Yes and a name
blocks.q: Add commas: “Yes Ms. Park I finished the book.”
steps: Yes starts the sentence: comma after it.
Ms. Park is the person spoken to, in the middle: commas on both sides.
blocks.a: Yes, Ms. Park, I finished the book.

blocks.html: Forgetting the second comma: “On May 4, 2025 the library opened.” A year or a state in the middle of a sentence is closed off on both sides, like a pair of brackets. The other common slip is leaving out the comma of direct address, which can change the meaning.

blocks.html: In Simple and Compound Sentences you joined two independent clauses with a coordinating conjunction: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so (FANBOYS). When one of these words joins two clauses that could each stand alone, a comma goes before it.

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: The rain stopped, and the children ran outside.

blocks.cap: Two subjects, two verbs: a compound sentence, so a comma comes before and.

blocks.html: Comma + and, but, or, so, yet, for or nor joins two independent clauses. If the word after the conjunction is not the start of a new subject and verb (a compound verb), leave the comma out.

The comma warns the reader that a second subject is coming. Without it, a reader may misread for a moment: “I painted the fence and my brother painted the shed” starts out sounding as if I painted both the fence and my brother. William Strunk’s fourth rule (1918) was: “Place a comma before a conjunction introducing a co-ordinate clause.”

blocks.title: Two clauses
blocks.q: “She ran to the corner and she waved at the bus.”
steps: Cover the and. Can each side stand alone?
“She ran to the corner.” Yes. “She waved at the bus.” Yes: it has its own subject, she.
Two independent clauses, so put a comma before and.
blocks.a: She ran to the corner, and she waved at the bus.

blocks.title: One subject, two verbs
blocks.q: “She ran to the corner and waved at the bus.”
steps: Cover the and. “Waved at the bus” has no subject of its own.
It is one clause with a compound verb: ran and waved.
No comma.
blocks.a: She ran to the corner and waved at the bus.

blocks.html: Putting a comma before every and: “She ran, and jumped.” Check the words right after the conjunction. A new subject (she, the dog, my brother) means a comma; a verb with no new subject means no comma.
Many style guides let you leave out this comma when both clauses are very short (“I knocked and she answered”). In school writing, using it is always correct.

blocks.html: Many sentences start with a warm-up before the main clause: a dependent clause (an adverb clause like “When the bell rang”), a long phrase, or a single word like However or Yes. A comma marks where the warm-up ends and the main clause begins.

blocks.name: wr-punct

opts.text: While we were eating the dog barked at the mail carrier.
answer: While we were eating, the dog barked at the mail carrier.

blocks.cap: Where does the opener end? Add the comma.

blocks.html: Use a comma after an opening dependent clause, an opening phrase of more than a few words, or an opening word like however, yes or well. After a short opening phrase, the comma is optional.

head: Opener
Comma?
rows: After the long game on Saturday, …

blocks.html: Without the comma, a reader can stumble: “While we were eating the dog barked” sounds, for a moment, as if we were eating the dog. The comma shows where the main sentence starts.

blocks.title: A long opening phrase
blocks.q: “After the long game on Saturday afternoon we went out for pizza.”
steps: Find the main clause: “we went out for pizza.”
Everything before it is an opening phrase of seven words.
Put the comma where the opener ends, after afternoon.
blocks.a: After the long game on Saturday afternoon, we went out for pizza.

blocks.title: The clause comes last
blocks.q: “We packed our bags when the bell rang.”
steps: The dependent clause “when the bell rang” comes after the main clause.
At the end of a sentence, a dependent clause usually takes no comma.
blocks.a: No comma: “We packed our bags when the bell rang.”

blocks.html: Leaving out the comma after a long opener, so the reader trips. The opposite worry is not a mistake: after a short opening phrase, “In 2020 we moved” and “In 2020, we moved” are both standard.

blocks.html: When two or more adjectives come before a noun, sometimes a comma goes between them and sometimes not. Coordinate adjectives each describe the noun on their own, like items in a series: “a long, cold winter.” Cumulative adjectives build on each other in a set order: “a big red barn.”
Two tests: switch the order, or put and between them. If both still sound natural, the adjectives are coordinate: use a comma. If not, they are cumulative: no comma.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.why: A cold and long winter: both tests work.
A red big barn sounds wrong.
A patient and quiet teacher: both tests work.
Small three puppies sounds wrong.
A stone old wall sounds wrong.

blocks.cap: Use the two tests on each card.

blocks.html: The comma stands for the and you could say: “a long and cold winter.” In a cumulative pair, the first adjective describes the whole phrase after it: in “a big red barn,” big describes the red barn. English puts such adjectives in a usual order (number, opinion, size, age, color, material), which is why switching them sounds wrong.

blocks.title: Coordinate
blocks.q: “a bright cheerful kitchen”
steps: Switch: “a cheerful bright kitchen.” Sounds fine.
Add and: “a bright and cheerful kitchen.” Sounds fine.
Both tests pass, so use a comma.
blocks.a: a bright, cheerful kitchen

blocks.title: Cumulative
blocks.q: “a shiny new bike”
steps: Switch: “a new shiny bike.” Possible, but it changes the stress.
Add and: “a shiny and new bike.” Odd.
The and test fails, so no comma.
blocks.a: a shiny new bike

blocks.html: Putting a comma between every pair of adjectives, or after the last one: “a long, cold, winter.” Never put a comma between the last adjective and its noun.

blocks.html: You know appositives and adjective clauses. Some of them are extra (nonessential): the sentence already tells us who or what. Others are essential: they tell us which one. Extra information gets a pair of commas; essential information gets none.

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: My brother, who lives in Ohio, is visiting.

blocks.cap: Cross out the extra part: “My brother is visiting.” We still know who.

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: The students who finished early went outside.

blocks.cap: Without “who finished early,” we don’t know which students went outside.

blocks.html: Take the words out. If the sentence still names exactly who or what, the words are extra: set them off with commas. If the sentence no longer tells which one, they are essential: no commas.

The commas change the meaning. “My sister who lives in Texas is a nurse” suggests you have more than one sister and are pointing to the one in Texas. “My sister, who lives in Texas, is a nurse” says you have one sister, and by the way she lives in Texas. Strunk’s third rule (1918): “Enclose parenthetic expressions between commas.”

blocks.title: A name already identifies
blocks.q: “Mount Rainier which is in Washington is a volcano.”
steps: Take out “which is in Washington”: “Mount Rainier is a volcano.”
The name already tells us which mountain, so the clause is extra.
Put commas on both sides of it.
blocks.a: Mount Rainier, which is in Washington, is a volcano.

blocks.title: An essential appositive
blocks.q: “The author Louisa May Alcott wrote Little Women.”
steps: Take out the name: “The author wrote Little Women.” Which author?
The name tells which one, so it is essential.
No commas.
blocks.a: No commas: “The author Louisa May Alcott wrote Little Women.”

blocks.html: Using only one comma (“My brother, who lives in Ohio is visiting”). Extra information in the middle of a sentence needs a pair. Which or that? American usage guides prefer that for essential clauses and which, with commas, for extra ones. Which in an essential clause (“the book which I lent you”) is standard too, especially in British English; it isn’t an error.

blocks.html: A period makes a full stop. A semicolon (;) is a softer stop that says “these two belong together.” It joins two independent clauses without a conjunction, the same kind of clauses you joined with a comma and and in Commas in Compound Sentences.

blocks.name: wr-combine

joins.label: ; (semicolon)
joins.make: The museum was closed; we went to the park.
joins.why: Two independent clauses, closely related: a semicolon works.

joins.label: , (comma only)
joins.make: The museum was closed, we went to the park.
joins.why: A comma alone can’t join two independent clauses: that is a comma splice.

joins.label: ; instead,
joins.make: The museum was closed; instead, we went to the park.
joins.why: Instead is not a conjunction, so it takes a semicolon before it and a comma after.

joins.label: , so
joins.make: The museum was closed, so we went to the park.
joins.why: A comma and a coordinating conjunction work too.

blocks.cap: Tap each way of joining the two sentences.

blocks.html: Use a semicolon (1) between two closely related independent clauses, (2) before a word like however, therefore or instead that joins two clauses, with a comma after that word, and (3) between items in a list when the items already have commas.
The semicolon lets a writer show that two ideas are linked without spelling out how. In a list, it acts as a bigger comma, so the reader can see where each item ends.

blocks.title: A list with commas inside
blocks.q: “We visited Akron, Ohio, Boise, Idaho, and Reno, Nevada.”
steps: Each item is a city and a state, with its own comma inside.
With commas between the items too, the reader can’t tell where one place ends.
Use semicolons between the items.
blocks.a: We visited Akron, Ohio; Boise, Idaho; and Reno, Nevada.

blocks.title: Before however
blocks.q: “It rained all morning however the game went on.”
steps: Two independent clauses: “It rained all morning” and “the game went on.”
However is not a conjunction, so it can’t join them alone.
Semicolon before it, comma after it.
blocks.a: It rained all morning; however, the game went on.

blocks.html: Using a semicolon where a colon or a comma belongs: before a list (“I need three things; flour, eggs and milk”) or after a dependent clause (“Because it rained; we stayed inside”). The test: could you put a period there instead? If not, don’t use a semicolon (unless you are separating list items that contain commas).

blocks.html: A colon (:) works like an arrow. The part before it is a complete sentence that promises something; the part after it delivers: a list, an explanation or a quotation. Like the semicolon, it needs a complete sentence in front of it.

blocks.name: wr-punct

opts.text: Bring three things a pencil, an eraser, and a ruler.
answer: Bring three things: a pencil, an eraser, and a ruler.

blocks.cap: Which gap gets the colon?

blocks.html: Use a colon after a complete sentence to introduce a list, an explanation or a quotation. Don’t put a colon right after a verb (are, is, include) or a preposition (of, such as).

The colon tells the reader, “Here it comes.” That only makes sense after words that are already complete: “I have two favorite fruits” sets up the list; “My favorite fruits are” is still waiting for its own words.

blocks.title: Fix a colon after a verb
blocks.q: “My favorite fruits are: apples and pears.”
steps: Cover everything after the colon: “My favorite fruits are.” That is not a complete sentence.
Either drop the colon or rewrite the first part as a complete sentence.
blocks.a: “My favorite fruits are apples and pears.” or “I have two favorite fruits: apples and pears.”

blocks.title: An explanation and a quotation
blocks.q: Where do the colons go?
steps: “The answer was clear: we needed a bigger tent.” The second part explains the first.
“Strunk’s second rule is short: ‘In a series of three or more terms with a single conjunction, use a comma after each term except the last.’” A complete sentence introduces the quotation.
blocks.a: After “clear” and after “short.”

blocks.html: Putting a colon after a verb or a preposition (“The kit includes: …”, “made of: …”, “such as: …”). Test: cover everything after the colon. If what is left isn’t a complete sentence, take the colon out. Colons also have a few set jobs: times (10:30), and the greeting of a formal letter (“Dear Ms. Park:”), where the colon is traditional.

blocks.html: A possessive noun shows that something belongs to someone: the dog’s bone. You know kinds of nouns and plurals; the trick with possessives is to start from the right form of the owner word, one or more than one.

head: Owner
Rule
Possessive
rows: plural ends in s: add ’ only
plural ends in s: add ’ only

blocks.html: Write the owner word first, singular or plural, exactly as it is. If it is plural and ends in s, add only an apostrophe. Otherwise add ’s.
In speech, “the girl’s coats” and “the girls’ coats” sound the same. On the page, the apostrophe’s place tells the reader how many owners there are: one girl, or many.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.why: The apostrophe comes after the plural s: many cats.
Children is already plural; it adds ’s.

blocks.cap: Look at where the apostrophe sits.

blocks.title: A plural owner
blocks.q: Write it as a possessive: “the toys of the babies”
steps: The owner word: babies. Plural, ends in s.
Add only an apostrophe.
blocks.a: the babies’ toys

blocks.title: An irregular plural
blocks.q: Write it as a possessive: “the hats of the men”
steps: The owner word: men. Plural, but it doesn’t end in s.
Add ’s.
blocks.a: the men’s hats

blocks.html: Using an apostrophe to make a plural: “Apple’s for sale.” A plural takes no apostrophe: “Apples for sale.” Names ending in s: guides differ. Chicago and MLA write James’s; AP writes James’. Purdue OWL recommends James’s and accepts James’. Use one style consistently.

blocks.html: A contraction squeezes two words into one, and the apostrophe stands where letters were left out: do not → don’t. It is a different job from the apostrophe in possessives, and mixing the two up causes the most famous slip in English: its and it’s.

head: Two words
Contraction
Letters left out
rows: an odd one: the word changes

blocks.html: The apostrophe goes exactly where letters are missing. It’s always means it is or it has. Its, meaning “belonging to it,” has no apostrophe, just like his, hers and ours.

blocks.name: wr-punct

opts.text: The cat licked it’s paw because its hungry.
opts.answer: The cat licked its paw because it’s hungry.
opts.hint: Tap its or it’s to switch it. Then Check.

blocks.cap: Fix the two words. Read “it is” in each place to test.

blocks.html: A reader uses the apostrophe to rebuild the full words. If it’s appears where no “it is” fits, the reader stumbles.

blocks.title: Its or it’s?
blocks.q: “The team lost (its / it’s) first game.”
steps: Try the long form: “The team lost it is first game.” That makes no sense.
So the word means “belonging to it”: no apostrophe.
blocks.a: The team lost its first game.

blocks.title: Where does the apostrophe go?
blocks.q: “does’nt” or “doesn’t”?
steps: The two words are does not.
The letter left out is the o in not.
The apostrophe takes its place.
blocks.a: doesn’t

blocks.html: Writing it’s for the possessive. Read “it is” in its place; if that doesn’t fit, write its. Contractions themselves are fine in most writing. Some teachers ask for full forms in formal essays, so follow the assignment.

blocks.html: Quotation marks go around a speaker’s exact words. With them come a few rules about the commas, periods and question marks nearby. You already set off spoken names with commas; dialogue uses commas too.

items: A comma separates the speaker tag from the words: Mia said, “We won.” “We won,” Mia said.
In American style, periods and commas go inside the closing mark.
A question mark or exclamation point goes inside only when the quotation itself asks or exclaims: Sam asked, “Where is the map?”
Start a new paragraph each time the speaker changes.
A quotation split by a tag doesn’t start again with a capital: “If it rains,” Mia said, “we’ll stay in.”

blocks.name: wr-revise

segments.why: American style: the comma goes inside the closing quotation mark.
The tag continues the sentence, so it isn’t capitalized.

blocks.cap: Two fixes to one line of dialogue.

blocks.html: Quote exact words. Periods and commas go inside the closing mark. Question marks and exclamation points go inside only when they belong to the quoted words. A new speaker gets a new paragraph.
Readers need to know exactly whose words they are reading and where those words stop. Keeping the marks in fixed places lets the reader stop thinking about punctuation and follow the conversation.

blocks.title: Whose question is it?
blocks.q: Punctuate: Did Ms. Park say “The test is on Friday”
steps: Ms. Park’s words are a statement, not a question.
The whole sentence is the question.
So the question mark goes outside the closing mark, and the quoted statement loses its period.
blocks.a: Did Ms. Park say, “The test is on Friday”?

blocks.title: Not exact words
blocks.q: “Mia said that she was ready.”
steps: These are not Mia’s exact words; the sentence reports what she said.
An indirect quotation takes no quotation marks.
blocks.a: No quotation marks needed.

blocks.html: Putting the comma or period outside: “Hi”, she said. That is common in British style, but American style puts it inside: “Hi,” she said. Also watch for a question mark placed inside when the quoted words don’t ask anything.

blocks.html: Titles are names, so they get capital letters. They also get a mark that shows what kind of work they name. Long works, and works that hold smaller parts, are in italics. Short works, and parts of bigger works, are in “quotation marks,” as with quoted words.

head: Italics (long works)
Quotation marks (short works and parts)
rows: articles in a newspaper or magazine
a short story: “The Tell-Tale Heart”; a chapter

blocks.html: Italicize the titles of long works (books, newspapers, magazines, movies, TV series, albums). Put the titles of short works and parts (poems, short stories, articles, songs, chapters, episodes) in quotation marks. In handwriting, underline what you would italicize.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.why: A chapter is part of a bigger work.
The article is part of the magazine; the magazine’s name goes in italics.

blocks.cap: Long work or short part?

blocks.html: The two marks show size and belonging. A song in quotation marks can sit on an album in italics; a chapter in quotation marks sits in a book in italics. The reader can tell at a glance which is the whole and which is the part.

blocks.title: A part and its whole
blocks.q: Punctuate the titles: Read the chapter Storms at Sea in the book Wild Waters. (made-up titles)
steps: Storms at Sea is a chapter, a part: quotation marks.
Wild Waters is the book, the whole: italics.
blocks.a: Read the chapter “Storms at Sea” in the book Wild Waters.

blocks.html: Putting a book title in quotation marks. Ask: is it a whole long work, or a short work or part? When you write by hand, you can’t make italics, so underline the title instead: <u>Little Women</u>.

blocks.html: You can set off extra information with commas. Two other marks do the same job in a different tone of voice. The dash (—) is loud: it makes a sharp break or stresses what it sets off. Parentheses ( ) are quiet: they tuck in an aside. An ellipsis (…) shows that words were left out.

head: Mark
Same sentence
Effect
rows: Our dog, a very old beagle, still chases squirrels.
Our dog—a very old beagle—still chases squirrels.
Our dog (a very old beagle) still chases squirrels.

blocks.name: wr-revise

segments.why: A dash makes the aside louder than a comma does.
In the middle of a sentence, dashes come in pairs.

blocks.cap: From commas to dashes: same words, more stress.

blocks.html: Dashes set off a sharp break or something to stress; parentheses set off a quieter extra; an ellipsis marks words left out of a quotation, or a trailing pause. A dash is not a hyphen: the hyphen (-) is short and joins words.
These marks let a writer control emphasis. If everything is set off with dashes, nothing stands out, so save the dash for the one thing you want the reader to notice.

blocks.title: A dash at the end
blocks.q: “There was only one thing left to do, run.”
steps: The last word is a sharp turn, and the writer wants it to land.
A dash gives it that weight.
blocks.a: There was only one thing left to do—run.

blocks.title: Shortening a quotation
blocks.q: Strunk wrote: “In a series of three or more terms with a single conjunction, use a comma after each term except the last.” Leave out “with a single conjunction.”
steps: Take out the words, keeping the meaning the same.
Put an ellipsis where the words were.
blocks.a: “In a series of three or more terms … use a comma after each term except the last.”

blocks.title: Parentheses and the period
blocks.q: “We hiked for six hours (with two short breaks).”
steps: The words in parentheses are part of the sentence.
So the period goes outside the closing parenthesis.
blocks.a: We hiked for six hours (with two short breaks).

blocks.html: Typing a hyphen for a dash (“I was tired - very tired”). Most word processors turn two hyphens into a dash, or you can insert the em dash (—) from the symbols menu. Also: a dash in the middle of a sentence needs a partner, just like a pair of commas, and an ellipsis must never change what the original said.

blocks.html: The dash separates; the hyphen (-) joins. Its main job is to show that two or more words work together as one describing word in front of a noun: a well-known author.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.why: Before the noun: a well-known author.
After the noun, usually no hyphen.
An -ly adverb takes no hyphen.
a ten-minute walk
forty-two

blocks.cap: Hyphen or not?

blocks.html: Hyphenate a compound modifier before a noun (a two-story house); usually not after it (the house is two stories tall). Never hyphenate after an -ly adverb (a brightly lit room). Hyphenate the numbers twenty-one to ninety-nine when you write them as words.

A hyphen can change the meaning. A small-animal doctor treats small animals; a small animal doctor could be a doctor who is small. A man-eating shark is dangerous; a man eating shark is a man having lunch.

blocks.title: Before and after the noun
blocks.q: “a ten year old boy” and “The boy is ten years old.”
steps: In the first, ten year old works as one adjective before boy: hyphens.
In the second, the words come after the noun as a phrase: no hyphens.
blocks.a: a ten-year-old boy; The boy is ten years old.

blocks.title: Numbers
blocks.q: Write 36 and 125 in words.
steps: Thirty-six is between twenty-one and ninety-nine: hyphen.
In 125, only the twenty-five part gets one.
blocks.a: thirty-six; one hundred twenty-five

blocks.html: Hyphenating after an -ly adverb (“a newly-built house”). The -ly already tells the reader that the word describes the next one, so style guides say no hyphen. Some words have hyphens of their own (self-aware, ex-coach, all-star); when in doubt, check a dictionary.

blocks.html: In Independent and Dependent Clauses you saw that only an independent clause can stand alone. A fragment is a piece of a sentence punctuated as if it were whole: it starts with a capital and ends with a period, but something is missing.

items: No subject: “Ran all the way to the bus.” (Who ran?)
No verb, or only an -ing word: “The man with the green umbrella.” “Running for the bus.” (See participles.)
A dependent clause alone: “Because it rained.” “When the game ended.” “Which surprised everyone.”

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: We stayed inside. Because it rained.

blocks.cap: The second piece has a subject and a verb, but because makes it dependent.

blocks.html: Every sentence needs a subject, a verb and at least one independent clause. A capital letter and a period don’t make a sentence.

A fragment leaves the reader waiting: because it rained, what? Strunk’s sixth rule (1918) was “Do not break sentences in two,” or, as he put it, “do not use periods for commas.” Most fragments are pieces broken off the sentence next to them, so the fix is usually to join them back.

blocks.title: Join a dependent clause
blocks.q: “We left early. Because the roads were icy.”
steps: “Because the roads were icy” has a subject and a verb, but because makes it dependent.
It belongs to the sentence before it.
Join them (no comma needed when the because-clause comes last).
blocks.a: We left early because the roads were icy.

blocks.title: Join an -ing phrase
blocks.q: “Running for the bus. I dropped my lunch.”
steps: “Running for the bus” has no subject and no full verb.
Attach it to the next sentence as an opener, with a comma.
Check that the subject right after it is the one running: I. Good.
blocks.a: Running for the bus, I dropped my lunch.

blocks.title: Add a verb
blocks.q: “The man with the green umbrella.”
steps: There is a subject, the man, but no verb.
Add what he does.
blocks.a: The man with the green umbrella waved to us.

blocks.html: Writing a dependent clause or an -ing phrase as a sentence, often right after the sentence it belongs to. Read each sentence alone, out of order: does it make a whole statement? Writers sometimes use a fragment on purpose for effect (“Not a chance.”), in stories and ads. In school and formal writing, use complete sentences.
