blocks.html: A run-on, also called a fused sentence, is the opposite of a fragment: two independent clauses run together with no punctuation and no joining word between them. You learned how to join clauses properly in Simple and Compound Sentences.

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: The bus was late we walked to school.

blocks.cap: Eight words, and a run-on: two subjects, two verbs, and nothing between the clauses.

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: After the rain finally stopped on Saturday afternoon, the children ran outside and splashed in every puddle they could find.

blocks.cap: Twenty words, and correct: one independent clause, properly joined to the rest.

blocks.html: A run-on has two independent clauses with nothing joining them. It is about how clauses are joined, not about length: a short sentence can be a run-on, and a long sentence can be correct.
Without a signal, the reader can’t tell where one thought ends: “Mia called her brother answered” reads at first as if Mia called her brother. Punctuation shows the border.

blocks.title: Find the border
blocks.q: “The store was closed we went home.”
steps: Look for a second subject and verb: we went.
The first clause ends just before it, after closed.
Nothing marks the border, so it is a run-on. The simplest fix is a period.
blocks.a: The store was closed. We went home.

blocks.title: Long but correct
blocks.q: “My grandmother, who grew up on a farm in Iowa, still wakes up before sunrise and makes coffee for everyone in the house.”
steps: Find the subjects and verbs: grandmother wakes … and makes; who grew up is inside a dependent clause.
Only one independent clause.
Long, but not a run-on.
blocks.a: Correct as written.

blocks.html: Thinking a run-on means a long sentence, and chopping good long sentences into short ones. Test: count the independent clauses, then check what joins them. Ways to fix them come in Five Ways to Fix a Run-On.

blocks.html: A comma splice is a run-on with a comma at the border: “It rained, we stayed inside.” In Commas in Compound Sentences the comma came with a conjunction; here it is alone, and alone it can’t do the job.

blocks.name: wr-combine

joins.label: , (comma only)
joins.why: A comma splice: a comma alone can’t join two independent clauses.

joins.label: , however
joins.make: It rained, however we played inside.
joins.why: Still a splice: however is not a conjunction.

joins.label: , so
joins.make: It rained, so we played inside.
joins.why: A comma with a coordinating conjunction joins the clauses.

joins.label: ; (semicolon)
joins.why: A semicolon can join two independent clauses on its own.

blocks.cap: Which joins work?

blocks.html: A comma alone can’t join two independent clauses. Words like however, then, therefore and also are not conjunctions, so a comma before them still makes a splice.

A comma tells the reader the sentence continues as one thought; a new subject right after it surprises them. Strunk’s fifth rule (1918) is “Do not join independent clauses by a comma.” He allowed one exception: “If the clauses are very short, and are alike in form, a comma is usually permissible,” as in “Man proposes, God disposes.” In school writing, use a stronger joint.

blocks.title: Spot the splice
blocks.q: “The movie was long, we enjoyed it anyway.”
steps: Cover the comma. “The movie was long.” Whole. “We enjoyed it anyway.” Whole.
Two independent clauses with only a comma between them: a comma splice.
One fix: add a conjunction.
blocks.a: The movie was long, but we enjoyed it anyway.

blocks.title: The however trap
blocks.q: “It rained, however we played outside.”
steps: However is a conjunctive adverb, not a conjunction.
So the comma is still joining two independent clauses alone.
Put a semicolon before however and a comma after it.
blocks.a: It rained; however, we played outside.

blocks.title: Not a splice
blocks.q: “When it rained, we played inside.”
steps: “When it rained” is a dependent clause.
A comma after an opening dependent clause is right.
blocks.a: Correct as written.

blocks.html: Joining clauses with a comma and a word like however or then: “We ate dinner, then we washed the dishes.” Fix it with and then, a semicolon, or a period.

blocks.html: Once you can spot a run-on or a comma splice, you have five ways to fix it. Each one shows the reader a slightly different link between the two ideas.

head: Fix
Example
What it shows
rows: The lights went out. We lit candles.
2. A comma and a coordinating conjunction
The lights went out, so we lit candles.
The lights went out; we lit candles.
When the lights went out, we lit candles.
time, cause or contrast (when, because, although)
5. A colon (if the second explains the first)
We had one choice: we lit candles.
the second part explains the first

blocks.name: wr-combine

joins.label: . (period)
joins.make: My phone died. I forgot to charge it.

joins.label: because
joins.make: My phone died because I forgot to charge it.
joins.why: Because makes the second clause dependent and shows the cause.

joins.label: : (colon)
joins.make: My phone died: I forgot to charge it.
joins.why: The second clause explains the first, so a colon works.

joins.label: , however,
joins.make: My phone died, however, I forgot to charge it.
joins.why: A comma before however still splices, and however (a contrast) is the wrong link here.

joins.label: , (comma only)
joins.make: My phone died, I forgot to charge it.

blocks.cap: Five tries; which fixes work?

blocks.html: Fix a run-on with a period, a comma plus and, but, or, so, yet, for, nor, a semicolon, a subordinating word, or a colon when the second clause explains the first. Before however or therefore, use a semicolon or a period, not a comma.

Choosing the fix is a writing decision. “It snowed. School closed.” is blunt. “Because it snowed, school closed.” shows cause. “It snowed; school closed.” lets the reader make the link. The meaning stays; the emphasis changes.

blocks.title: Fix a splice with however
blocks.q: “The test was hard, however I passed.”
steps: Two independent clauses; however is not a conjunction.
Semicolon before however, comma after it.
Or use a conjunction: “The test was hard, but I passed.”
blocks.a: The test was hard; however, I passed.

blocks.title: Choose the link
blocks.q: “We were tired we kept walking.”
steps: The ideas contrast: tired, yet still walking.
A contrast word fits: but, yet or although.
blocks.a: We were tired, but we kept walking. (or: Although we were tired, we kept walking.)

blocks.html: Fixing a splice by putting a comma before however: “It rained, however, we played.” That is still a splice. A conjunctive adverb needs a semicolon or a period before it. And a colon only works when the second clause explains or completes the first.

blocks.html: In a series, each item should take the same grammatical form: all -ing words, all infinitives (to + verb), all nouns, or all clauses. This is called parallel structure.

blocks.name: wr-revise

segments: On Saturdays I like hiking, swimming, and

segments.why: The other two items are -ing words, so the third one should be too.

blocks.cap: One item out of step, fixed.

blocks.html: Make every item in a list or series the same kind of grammar. If the first is an -ing word, they all are; if the first is to + verb, they all are.

A parallel list has a rhythm the reader can hear, and the matching forms show that the items are equals. A mismatched item trips the reader. Strunk’s fifteenth rule (1918): “Express co-ordinate ideas in similar form.”

blocks.title: Infinitives
blocks.q: “The coach told us to stretch, to drink water, and that we should rest.”
steps: The first two items are infinitives: to stretch, to drink water.
The third is a clause: that we should rest.
Make it an infinitive too.
blocks.a: The coach told us to stretch, to drink water, and to rest.

blocks.title: Nouns
blocks.q: “The job needs patience, being careful, and a sense of humor.”
steps: Patience and a sense of humor are nouns; being careful is an -ing phrase.
Find a noun for it: care.
blocks.a: The job needs patience, care, and a sense of humor.

blocks.html: With infinitives you may repeat to or not: “to hike, swim, and ride” and “to hike, to swim, and to ride” are both parallel.

Mixing forms in a list: “to hike, swimming, and a bike ride.” Read the start of the sentence with each item alone: “I like to hike. I like swimming. I like a bike ride.” When the forms change, rewrite to match.

blocks.html: Parallel structure matters in pairs too. Correlative conjunctions come in pairs: both … and, either … or, neither … nor, not only … but also, whether … or. Whatever follows the first word must match what follows the second.

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: She plays not only the piano but also the violin.

blocks.cap: Each half of the pair is followed by the same kind of words.

blocks.html: Put each half of a correlative pair right before matching words: noun with noun, verb with verb, phrase with phrase. In comparisons with than or as, compare like with like.
A pair works like a balance scale: each pan must hold the same kind of thing. Strunk wrote in 1918 that correlative expressions “should be followed by the same grammatical construction.”

blocks.title: Move the first half
blocks.q: “She not only plays the piano but also the violin.”
steps: After not only: plays the piano, a verb phrase.
After but also: the violin, a noun.
Move not only so a noun follows it too.
blocks.a: She plays not only the piano but also the violin.

blocks.title: Either … or
blocks.q: “Either you can walk or take the bus.”
steps: After either: you can walk, a whole clause.
After or: take the bus, a verb phrase.
Move either next to the verb.
blocks.a: You can either walk or take the bus.

blocks.title: A comparison
blocks.q: “Ana’s grades are higher than Ben.”
steps: The sentence compares grades with … Ben himself.
Compare grades with grades.
blocks.a: Ana’s grades are higher than Ben’s.

blocks.html: Putting the first half of the pair too early, as in “She not only plays the piano but also the violin.” Find the two halves and read what comes right after each; the two must match. In comparisons, check that you compare the same kinds of things: “Swimming is harder than running,” not “than to run.”

blocks.html: A capital letter marks a name: a particular person, place or thing. You have used capitals since names of people and pets; here are the rules that trip up older writers. They rest on the difference between proper and common nouns.

head: Capitalize
Don’t capitalize
rows: Aunt Rosa, Mom (used as a name)
Mayor Diaz, Doctor Rivera (title before a name)

blocks.name: wr-punct

opts.text: last summer my uncle drove us south to visit aunt rosa in atlanta, georgia.
answer: Last summer my uncle drove us south to visit Aunt Rosa in Atlanta, Georgia.
opts.hint: Tap a word to switch its capital letter. Then Check.

blocks.cap: Fix the capitals. Leave the words that aren’t names alone.

blocks.html: Capitalize proper nouns and the adjectives made from them, titles right before a name, family words used as names, and the names of regions. Don’t capitalize seasons, compass directions, titles used alone, or family words after my, your or our.
Capitals let a reader tell a name from an ordinary word: “the South” is a region; “south” is a direction. “Mom called” uses Mom as her name; “my mom called” uses mom as an ordinary noun.

blocks.title: Family words
blocks.q: “Mom and my dad came to the game.”
steps: Mom is used as a name (you could put her name there): capital.
my dad follows my, so it is an ordinary noun: small letter.
blocks.a: Correct as written: Mom, my dad.

blocks.title: Directions and regions
blocks.q: “We drove North to visit friends in the midwest.”
steps: north is a direction: lowercase.
the Midwest names a region: capital.
blocks.a: We drove north to visit friends in the Midwest.

blocks.html: Capitalizing ordinary nouns for emphasis (“the Best Game Ever”), a family word after my (“my Uncle”), or a direction (“drive North”). Ask: is this word a name, or could a or the go in front of it as an ordinary word?

blocks.html: When you write the title of a book, a song or your own essay, you use title case: the important words get capitals and the small connecting words don’t. It builds on capitalization and titles.

Capitalize the first word and every major word: nouns, pronouns, verbs (including short ones like Is and Be), adjectives and adverbs. Lowercase a, an, the, the conjunctions and, but, or, and short prepositions such as in, on, of, to, at, by in the middle of the title. Style guides differ on longer prepositions.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.why: Short, but a verb: capitalize.
Short, but a pronoun: capitalize.

blocks.cap: These follow every major style guide.

head: Preposition in the middle
Lowercase in
Capitalized in
rows: of, in, to, at (two or three letters)
about, under, through, between (five or more)
blocks.cap: Chicago Manual of Style (18th ed.), MLA Handbook (9th ed.), APA (7th ed.) and AP. Chicago’s 18th edition (2024) began capitalizing prepositions of five or more letters.

blocks.html: Title case makes a title stand out as a name. The guides agree on the big picture and differ on the edges, so the real rule is to know which guide your teacher, school or publisher uses, and follow it the same way every time.

blocks.title: All guides agree
blocks.q: “the secret of the old mill”
steps: First word: The.
Nouns and adjectives: Secret, Old, Mill.
Article and short preposition in the middle: of, the.
blocks.a: The Secret of the Old Mill

blocks.title: Guides differ
blocks.q: “a walk through the woods”
steps: A, Walk, Woods: capitals in every guide; the: lowercase.
through is a seven-letter preposition.
MLA lowercases it; Chicago (18th ed.), APA and AP capitalize it.
blocks.a: MLA: A Walk through the Woods. Chicago, APA, AP: A Walk Through the Woods.

blocks.html: Capitalizing every word (“The Secret Of The Old Mill”). Small words like of and the stay lowercase in the middle in all the major guides. One more difference: in an APA reference list, titles of articles and books use sentence case (only the first word and names capitalized).

blocks.html: Some words sound alike but mean different things. Several pairs are a contraction and a possessive word, so the apostrophe test you know will sort them out.

head: Word
Meaning
Example
rows: The dog wagged its tail. It’s late.
belonging to them / that place / they are
They’re putting their coats over there.
Who’s the girl whose bike this is?
Two of us went to the store too.
Taller than me; we ate, then left.

blocks.html: If a word has an apostrophe, read it as two words (it is, they are, you are, who is). If the two words don’t fit, use the form without the apostrophe. Use than to compare and then for time.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.why: They are coming at noon.
There is often used to start a sentence: there are, there is.

blocks.cap: Which word fills the blank?

blocks.html: A spell checker only knows whether a word is spelled right, not whether it is the word you meant: “Their going too the park” passes a spell check. A reader notices at once.

blocks.title: Three in one sentence
blocks.q: “___ going to bring ___ dog over ___.”
steps: First blank: “They are going”: They’re.
Second: the dog belongs to them: their.
Third: a place: there.
blocks.a: They’re going to bring their dog over there.

blocks.title: Then or than?
blocks.q: “She is taller ___ her brother, and ___ she grew another inch.”
steps: The first compares: than.
The second tells what happened next: then.
blocks.a: than; then

blocks.html: Trusting the spell checker. Proofread these words on purpose: expand every apostrophe word into two words, and check every then and than.

blocks.html: After the sound-alike words come pairs that look alike or are close in meaning. The Vocabulary Ladder has full pages for some of them: affect, effect, imply and infer.

head: Pair
The difference
Example
rows: affect is usually a verb (to influence); effect is usually a noun (a result)
The rain affected the game. It had a big effect.
accept: take or agree to; except: leaving out
We accept everyone except Sam’s cat.
the speaker implies (hints); the listener infers (concludes)
She implied it was late; I inferred we should go.
lose: misplace, not win; loose: not tight
complement: completes, goes well with; compliment: praise
The scarf complements her coat. He gave her a compliment.
fewer: things you count; less: amounts

blocks.html: Learn each pair by its job: affect is the action (a verb) and effect is the end result (a noun); the speaker implies and the listener infers; compliment is what I say to praise you.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.text: How will the storm ___ the trip?
The ___ of the change was clear.
cards.why: After the, a noun: effect.

blocks.cap: Verb or noun?

blocks.html: These pairs differ by a letter or two, but the meanings differ a lot, and a careful reader notices. Using the right one shows you know what you mean.

blocks.title: Affect or effect?
blocks.q: “The new rule will (affect / effect) every student.”
steps: After will, we need a verb.
Affect is the verb meaning to influence.
blocks.a: affect

blocks.title: Imply or infer?
blocks.q: “From her smile, I (implied / inferred) that she had won.”
steps: I am the one drawing a conclusion from what I see.
The listener or reader infers.
blocks.a: inferred

blocks.html: Mixing up words that look alike. Two pairs have rare second uses: effect can be a verb meaning “to bring about” (“to effect change”), and affect is a noun in psychology. Fewer and less: careful writers use fewer with things you count. Less with counts (“10 items or less”) is common and old, but many readers notice it in formal writing. With amounts of money, time and distance, less is standard: “less than five dollars.”

blocks.html: Some mistakes come from writing what we hear. In fast speech, could have sounds like “could of,” and supposed to sounds like “suppose to.” Formal writing uses the actual words. Like tricky pairs, these are about knowing what the words are.

head: What you may hear
What formal writing uses
rows: could of, should of, would of
could have (could’ve), should have, would have
all right (many editors still expect two words)

blocks.name: wr-revise

segments.why: Could’ve sounds like “could of,” but the word is have.
The -d is hard to hear before to, but it is there.
A lot is always two words.

blocks.cap: Three repairs in one sentence.

blocks.html: Write could have, should have and would have (or their contractions), supposed to and used to, a lot, all right and regardless in formal writing.

In speech, the sounds blur and no one minds. On the page, “could of” looks like a different grammar (could + of) and readers notice. Many people say these forms in conversation; formal written English uses the full forms.

blocks.title: Could of
blocks.q: “I should of studied for the quiz.”
steps: The helping verb after should is have.
“Should’ve” is the contraction, which sounds like “should of.”
blocks.a: I should have studied for the quiz. (or should’ve)

blocks.title: Used to
blocks.q: “We use to live in Ohio.”
steps: The meaning is a past habit.
The past form is used to; the -d is hard to hear before to.
blocks.a: We used to live in Ohio.

blocks.html: Writing what you hear: could of, alot, suppose to. Alright is common in informal writing and appears in dictionaries, but many teachers and editors still mark it in formal work, so all right is the safe choice. Irregardless is heard in speech; formal writing uses regardless.

blocks.html: Some “rules” you may have heard aren’t rules of English grammar at all. Three famous ones: never split an infinitive, never end a sentence with a preposition, and never start a sentence with And or But. Like singular they, these are places where you should know the range.

head: The old “rule”
What usage guides say
Example
rows: Don’t split an infinitive (to + adverb + verb).
Not an error. Split it when that reads more clearly.
She decided to quickly finish her homework.
Don’t end a sentence with a preposition.
Not an error. Often the natural choice.
Don’t start a sentence with And or But.
Not an error. Good writers have done it for centuries.

blocks.html: Splitting an infinitive, ending with a preposition and starting with And or But are standard English. Some teachers and readers still object, especially in formal writing, so know your audience and choose the version that reads best.

blocks.name: wr-sort

bins: Breaks a rule of standard grammar

cards.why: Ending with a preposition is not an error.

cards.text: The list of chores are long.
cards.why: The subject is list, so the verb is is.
Starting with But is not an error.

cards.text: She promised to carefully check each answer.
cards.why: A split infinitive is not an error.

cards.text: Each of the girls have a ticket.
cards.why: Each is singular: Each of the girls has a ticket.

cards.text: It was late, we went home.
cards.why: A comma splice.

blocks.cap: Myth or real rule?

blocks.html: Many of these bans come from grammar writers of the 1600s to 1800s who measured English against Latin. In Latin an infinitive is one word, so it can’t be split; English infinitives are two words. The Chicago Manual of Style accepts split infinitives and endings with a preposition, and in 2024 Merriam-Webster reminded readers that you can end a sentence with a preposition.

blocks.title: Ending with a preposition
blocks.q: “Who did you give it to?” or “To whom did you give it?”
steps: Both are grammatical.
The second sounds more formal; the first sounds natural.
Choose by the occasion, not by a rule.
blocks.a: Both are correct.

blocks.title: When splitting is clearer
blocks.q: “We expect our club to more than double in size.”
steps: Try moving more than: “to double more than in size” makes no sense.
Here the split infinitive is the clearest way to say it.
blocks.a: Keep the split.

blocks.title: A real error, for comparison
blocks.q: “The list of chores are long.”
steps: The subject is list, which is singular.
This breaks a real rule of standard grammar: subject–verb agreement.
blocks.a: The list of chores is long.

blocks.html: Treating old classroom bans as rules of grammar, and “correcting” good sentences into awkward ones (“That is something up with which I will not put”). The other mistake is assuming every reader agrees: some teachers still ask you to avoid these in formal essays. Follow the assignment, and know that the sentence is not wrong.
